title: Supreme Court Issues Ultimatum to FSSAI on Food Warning Labels
excerpt: India's top court told the Centre this is its 'last chance' to finalize front-of-pack warning labels on packaged foods high in sugar, salt, and saturated fat, giving FSSAI a fortnight to make a decision or face judicial action.
body:
• India's Supreme Court issued an ultimatum to the Centre and FSSAI, calling it the "last chance" to finalize front-of-pack warning labels on packaged foods high in sugar, salt, and saturated fat
  • The court gave FSSAI a fortnight to make a definitive decision, dismissing arguments about traditional foods and foreign standards, and prioritizing children's health
  • FSSAI has delayed action since April 2025 despite multiple court directives, citing lack of consensus on the Indian Nutrition Rating star-based system
  • India's overweight and obese adult population is projected to reach 449 million by 2050, and the country already has 101 million diabetes patients

Court Loses Patience With Delays

The Supreme Court of India has run out of patience with the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India's repeated delays on implementing front-of-pack warning labels for packaged foods. A bench comprising Justices JB Pardiwala and KV Viswanathan delivered a blunt ultimatum, telling the Centre this is its "last chance" to act on the public health measure.

The court gave FSSAI a fortnight to finalize its position on mandatory warning labels that would clearly flag foods high in sugar, sodium, and saturated fat. The justices dismissed industry arguments centered on traditional foods and foreign labelling standards, signaling that judicial intervention could follow if a definitive decision is not forthcoming.

"Whatever exercise has been undertaken so far has not yielded any positive or good result. The PIL raised an important issue as regards the right to health of the citizens of this country."

— Supreme Court bench of Justices Pardiwala and Viswanathan

A Timeline of Inaction

The case traces back to a public interest litigation filed by NGO 3S and Our Health Society in 2024, seeking directions for clear front-of-package warnings on processed foods. The original PIL was disposed of on April 9, 2025, after FSSAI assured the court it had begun work on front-of-pack nutrition labelling through amendments to the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020.

The court directed an FSSAI-appointed expert committee to submit recommendations within three months. When compliance was reviewed in February 2026, the bench found that FSSAI's affidavit — filed by Joint Director Dr. Kavitha Ramasamy — revealed no meaningful progress. The expert committee reported a lack of consensus among stakeholders on the proposed Indian Nutrition Rating, a star-based system ranging from 0.5 to 5 stars.

The affidavit also revealed that FSSAI had postponed the matter during its 49th meeting in November 2025, planning to revisit it later. The authority proposed conducting further consumer surveys, mapping packaged foods by category, and studying international trends before acting.

Public Health Crisis at Stake

The court's urgency reflects India's escalating public health crisis linked to diet. According to a Lancet study, India's overweight and obese adult population is projected to surge from 180 million in 2021 to 449 million by 2050 — the second-highest burden globally. A separate Indian Council of Medical Research study reported approximately 101 million Indians living with diabetes, making the country the world's diabetes capital.

The FSSAI's proposed labelling reform would target India's rapidly growing packaged food market, valued at over $121 billion. Health experts have pointed to successful models in Chile, Israel, and Brazil, where front-of-pack warning labels led to product reformulation and measurable improvements in public health outcomes.

Industry Resistance and the Path Forward

The petitioner's legal team, led by advocate Rajiv Shankar Dwivedi, argued that FSSAI had used consultations as a stalling tactic, noting the expert committee had not convened even once during the original three-month window. The petitioner advocated for clear warning labels over the star-rating system, arguing the latter obscures harmful content rather than flagging it transparently.

The court acknowledged these concerns, observing that front-of-pack warning labels are an internationally prevalent public health measure. If FSSAI fails to meet the latest deadline, the court has indicated it may initiate contempt proceedings — a prospect that could force the food authority's hand on one of the most significant public health interventions in recent Indian regulatory history.
